title: 10 Ways to Earn Passive Income With $0
description: No money? No problem. Here are 10 real ways I started earning passive income with just my time and smartphone, perfect for complete beginners.
alt: College student earning money on laptop with empty wallet nearby

content.text: Passive income has a marketing problem. Most of what's sold under that label takes a lot of work up front, pays slowly, and for plenty of people pays almost nothing. The ideas below cost nothing to start, which is their real appeal, but treat them as small side streams you build gradually rather than a replacement for a salary. Several of these platforms are also US-focused, so check that each one pays out where you live.
1. Sell Your Class Notes

If you take clear, well-organised notes, marketplaces like Stuvia and StudySoup will list them for other students, handle the payments and take a commission on each sale. Notes for STEM and business courses tend to find buyers more easily than most. Check your school's academic-integrity rules first, and don't upload material that's mostly your lecturer's slides or anything else you don't have the right to sell.
2. Simple Digital Products

Resume templates, meal planners and budget trackers made in Canva or Google Docs can be sold on platforms like Gumroad, which has no monthly fee and takes a cut of each sale. The trick is to solve one narrow problem for one kind of person, a weekly budget template for students, say, rather than making something generic. Build the design yourself, and read the platform's licence terms before selling anything made with its stock elements.
3. Sell Photos From Your Phone

Apps like Foap and Wirestock accept phone photos and pay when they're licensed; Wirestock sends your uploads on to several stock agencies. Earnings per photo are small, so this is closer to coffee money than a wage, and it only adds up if you upload steadily. Local landmarks, food and everyday objects are easier to sell than random snapshots, and anything showing recognisable people or private property needs permission.
4. Affiliate Links for Tools You Already Use

Plenty of tools run affiliate programs, Notion, Canva and Amazon among them. If you recommend one to people who'd genuinely use it, you earn a commission when they sign up or buy. Say it's an affiliate link every time. It isn't passive at the start, because someone has to see your links, and some programs, Amazon's included, close accounts that don't produce qualifying sales within a set period. Only recommend what you actually use.
5. Sell or Rent What You Already Own

Textbooks you've finished with can be sold for the best price by comparing buyback offers on BookScouter. Spare space can be rented out for events and photo shoots through sites like PeerSpace, which is mainly a US marketplace. Never rent out anything you couldn't afford to lose or replace.
6. Design for Print on Demand

On a site like Redbubble you upload artwork or lettering once, and the platform prints, ships and pays you a margin when someone buys a T-shirt, sticker or mug. There's no stock to hold and no cost to list. There is a lot of competition, though, so a distinct niche beats a broad one.
7. Turn What You Know Into a Short Guide

A 20-page guide on something you've worked out, such as budgeting on irregular income, can be sold on Gumroad or, if you're in Nigeria, on Selar. You write it once and every sale after that is automatic. Finding the readers is the part that takes effort.
8. Sell Royalty-Free Sounds

Video makers and podcasters buy ambient recordings like rain, street noise and café background. Stock-audio marketplaces such as Pond5 and AudioJungle accept submissions from independent creators and pay a share when a clip is licensed. A clean recording, with no stray speech or traffic, matters more than the equipment.
9. Get Paid for Everyday Data and Attention

Brave's browser pays out in its own token, BAT, if you opt in to its privacy-respecting ads, and Fetch Rewards turns scanned shopping receipts into gift cards, though Fetch is only available in the US. These earn very little, and they're the closest thing on this list to effortless. Stick to apps with clear privacy policies, because you're trading a little data for a small reward.
10. Repurpose What You've Already Made

Posts, threads and tips you've already written can keep working. Turn a strong thread into a short guide, or pin the best of it to Pinterest, where it can keep sending traffic to your products or affiliate links long after you published it. Evergreen advice, the kind that's still true next year, is what's worth repurposing.

content.text: This is a rough guide, not measured data, and results vary a great deal between people. The pattern worth noticing is that the ideas with the highest upfront effort tend to be the ones with the most room to grow, while the effortless ones barely pay. That's the usual trade-off with passive income: you either put in work now or accept very small returns.
How much time to expect to spend

Set aside a few focused hours a week for the first couple of months. Most of the work is front-loaded: creating, uploading and improving listings. After that, a monthly check-in to refresh what isn't selling and add a little more is usually enough. If an idea still isn't getting views after a few months of honest effort, it's reasonable to drop it and try another. Spending your time where something works beats loyalty to a plan that doesn't.
What these actually pay

Be realistic about the money. Most of these will earn little. Marketplaces pay per sale, so earnings depend on demand, competition and how much you've listed, and plenty of listings sit untouched for months. The people who do well usually have many listings, a narrow niche and a lot of patience, and they treat the first few months as practice. A sensible goal for your first quarter is a first sale, not a salary.
How to choose your first one

Start with what you already have: time, a skill, a phone, a laptop, a subject you know well. If you take good notes, start there. If you can design, start with templates or print on demand. If you're good at explaining things, write a short guide. Pick the idea where your first listing could be live this week, because a modest listing today teaches you more than a perfect plan next month.
Getting paid, and keeping it safe

Before you spend hours on any platform, check how it pays out. Many use PayPal, Payoneer or bank transfer, and availability differs by country, so confirm that your option works where you live. Remember that commissions and fees come off each sale, and that income from side projects may be taxable, so keep simple records of what you earn.

Be careful about scams in this space, too. Legitimate platforms don't charge you a fee to start earning. If a "job" asks you to pay to unlock tasks, deposit money to withdraw earnings, or cash a cheque and send some of it back, walk away. A real opportunity pays you; it doesn't ask you to pay first.
A simple first-month plan

items: Week 1: Choose one idea and set up your account on the relevant platform.
Week 2: Create and publish your first three listings, even if they're not perfect.
Week 3: Improve them using whatever you've learned, such as clearer titles, better previews or a tighter niche.
Week 4: Review what got views or sales, and decide whether to do more of it or try a second idea.

content.text: Beginner Mistakes to Avoid

Don't put everything into one method. Most of these earn little on their own and you won't know which suits you until you've tried a couple. Track your time as well, because some "passive" ideas quietly eat hours, and a stream that costs you an hour of upkeep for every few dollars isn't doing you much good. And treat anyone promising easy thousands for no money, skill or effort with suspicion; if it were that easy, everyone would already be doing it.
Making money is only half of it. Keeping it, and keeping your costs and losses down, matters just as much. If you want the wider picture, start with building wealth from scratch.
Pick one or two that fit skills you already have, give each a few months, and see what actually pays.

faq.question: Can I earn passive income with no money?
faq.answer: Yes, many ideas need no upfront cash, only time and effort. Expect small payments at first, and note that some platforms only pay out in certain countries.

faq.question: Do I really need only a smartphone to get started?
faq.answer: For a few of them, like photo uploads or receipt scanning, a smartphone is enough. Others, such as templates or short guides, are easier to build on a laptop.

faq.question: Is passive income truly passive?
faq.answer: Rarely at the start. Most streams need real work up front and some upkeep afterwards, so "semi-passive" is closer to the truth.

faq.question: How long does it take to earn passive income?
faq.answer: It varies a lot. Some people see a first small payment within weeks, others take months, and some never earn much. Choosing something people actually want matters more than speed.

faq.question: Are these passive income ideas suitable for complete beginners?
faq.answer: Yes, none of them need specialist skills, though a few call for basic design or writing ability. Results depend on effort and on whether there's demand for what you make.
